prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of uncertainty
for the conception of the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) paired with IceCube (Halzen). Round 1 moved me on B043 more than on anything else. Kroll's point that neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 single-quantum-system prize credited the idea of an ensemble of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice answers my overlap worry, and the independent confirmation in Sr, Yb and Hg is not disputed by anyone. It has the cleanest two-name credit on the shortlist and the broadest support in the room. I still think a prize that rests only on a measurement advance is thin, which is why I want a discovery-type partner. IceCube's diffuse TeV-PeV flux is a discovery of a new window on the universe, accepted as such by every member who commented, with the objections limited to credit. The one-name credit is the part I hold most loosely, and I answer the chair's question below.
statement.case_against: Three objections remain. First, a lone laureate for a collaboration of hundreds will look arbitrary to part of the community, and nobody in round 1 supplied a decisive individual contribution that separates Halzen from Karle and Yoshida. Second, B043 may still be read as refinement of a frequency-standard programme the Academy has honoured twice, and its headline application, the redefinition of the second, has not happened. Third, pairing two unrelated fields dilutes each, as Pearce also notes. If the committee judges the IceCube credit indefensible, the right fallback is B043 alone, not an invented trio, because the three-person cap does not allow Katori, Ye and a full IceCube credit together.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B043 plus IceCube credited to Halzen as the conceiver and leader, and concedes that the one-person credit is the weak point and that a single coherent achievement such as B043 alone would be cleaner.
responses.response: We hold the same configuration and the same doubt, so I want to be specific about where I stand on the chair's question. I cannot name a contribution that decisively separates Halzen from Karle and Yoshida. What I can say is that Halzen is the one name that the conception of a cubic-kilometre detector and the programme to the diffuse-flux discovery attach to most directly, while Karle's and Yoshida's roles lie more in construction and analysis leadership that a collaboration prize would normally absorb. That makes Halzen defensible but not inevitable, and I accept your point that B043 alone is the cleaner outcome if the committee cannot live with it. I would still not add Karle or Yoshida, because that forces out Katori or Ye.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes because neither credited an ensemble of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, and that two names map onto the concept and the record accuracy.
responses.response: That is the most useful argument against my own earlier hesitation and I accept it: removing Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating many atoms is a different limitation overcome, not a repeat of the comb. We differ on whether it suffices alone. I think the committee would be better served by a citation that names the 1e-18 performance as a demonstrated result, as you also want, but I remain unwilling to rest a whole year's prize on a measurement advance when a mature discovery of comparable standing is available. If the committee prefers B043 alone, I would not call that wrong, only less ambitious.

responses.point: Olsson prefers twisted bilayer graphene as a prediction followed by experiment and questions how robust the IceCube source associations are beyond the diffuse flux.
responses.response: On IceCube, my case rests on the diffuse flux, which was found by independent analysis channels, and not on TXS 0506+056 or NGC 1068, which I agree are at moderate significance. I would keep the citation on the discovery of the flux, as drafted. On B029 I still think the maturity concern stands: the experiments are from 2018 and the pairing mechanism is open. The credit also remains untidy, with Cao, Fatemi and Dean on the experimental side and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory. That is why it is my first alternative, not my preference, and I would revisit it in a few years.

responses.point: Eriksson answers my timing caution by saying a B029 citation would honour the flat bands and correlated insulating and superconducting phenomenology, not the unsettled mechanism.
responses.response: That narrows the citation helpfully, and I accept that the phenomenology is reproduced by many groups. My remaining doubt is that a prize rewarding a phenomenology whose explanation is still disputed risks being overtaken by later results, whereas the lattice clock and the diffuse neutrino flux are settled. I also note your view that the three-name structure maps cleanly onto theory plus experiment; the omission of Cao and Fatemi makes it less clean than it looks. I keep B029 as my first alternative for that reason and not as a rejection of the science.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers topological insulators for the Kane-Mele prediction and the HgTe observation, as a rare case of prediction followed by quantitative confirmation, while acknowledging the 2016 topological prize overlap and the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang problem.
responses.response: The prediction and confirmation structure is genuinely attractive, and I agree the physics is mature. I do not put it in my configuration because of the very overlap you raise: after 2016 the committee would have to argue that the Z2 classification is a separate principle from the topological phases honoured then, and the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang under a three-name cap compounds that. I would not rank it below B029 on science, only on how defensible the citation is this year.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen alone is defensible for IceCube. I could not identify a decisive individual contribution separating him from Karle and Yoshida, so this rests on judgement about conception and leadership, and on my memory of the credit history, which I have not verified against the nomination text.
Whether the committee prefers a single coherent achievement (B043 alone) to a two-part prize; I would accept B043 alone before an artificial IceCube trio.
Whether the lattice clock counts as a discovery in the sense the committee intends, and whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay it.
Whether GRB afterglows (B033) can be credited cleanly at all, given van Paradijs and the claims of Piro, Djorgovski, Metzger and Frail; I have not found a better attribution than the others have.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any shortlisted candidate, and I have no tie to Katori, Ye or Halzen. Round 1 raised no flag that changes this.
